sources.news_title: Buc-ee's founder hints at states that may become focus of future locations
Buc-ee's CEO Says His Beloved Gas Station Chain Will Likely Stay Away From Blue States, Moving Forward, As They Are So Anti-Business - The American Tribune.com
sources.text:
The CEO of popular gas station chain Buc-ee’s, recently stated that the Texas-based company might be through with looking into blue districts, stating that some of these communities do not appreciate what they bring to the table, while conservative states offer business-friendly and family-oriented values. Arch “Beaver” Aplin III, the company’s president, made the comments during the grand opening of a new Buc-ee’s location in Benton, Arkansas on August 17, 2026.
The chain is well known for its expansive gas stations, immaculate bathrooms, and wide selection of in-house food items. “We have a lot of opportunities. We’re growing. We’re building in a lot of places. But when you find a conservative business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference,” Aplin went on to say during the grand opening.
Aplin then ripped into states that he says do not appreciate what Buc-ee’s brings to their communities, suggesting the company would rather focus time and attention toward expanding elsewhere. Aplin stated that conservative states tend to promote business-friendly and family-oriented policies that align with his company’s values.
“I’m starting to realize life’s too short to try to build in places that people don’t appreciate what you’re bringing, versus a place like this where people do appreciate what you are building,” he said, according to a report from Fox Business. That leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept works so much better if it trickles down from the very leadership from the top at the governor’s office, at the congressman, at the senator, at the mayor, the representatives.”
Aplin then pointed to Benton as a prime example of the kind of approach that Buc-ee’s is looking for in a community, saying the business-friendly environment helped clear a path for the new location. “What we found when we got here into Benton was a business-friendly town,” he stated at the grand opening. Buc-ee’s was originally founded in 1982, with each location featuring a 74,000 square foot space with over 120 fueling positions.
When Buc-ee’s rolls into town, it brings with it over 200 jobs. The company currently has 58 locations, with 37 of those being in Texas, according to the company’s website. Buc-ee’s has expanded to 13 other states in the country including Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Arizona, Colorado, Mississippi, Missouri, Ohio, South Carolina and Virginia.
Almost all of the cities where Buc-ee’s has built one of its massive travel stations is located in a conservative-leaning area, with a few that are more mixed when it comes to political views and policies. There’s a store located in Auburn, Alabama for example, which is a college town located in a mostly Republican county, which is more politically mixed than many surrounding communities.
"*" indicates required fields
The store in Brunswick, Georgia is based in a more Democratic-leaning community, despite being seated in a Glynn County, which is usually more on the conservative side. As of this writing, more Buc-ee’s locations are slated to open including a travel center in Murfreesboro, Tennessee later this fall. Six locations are scheduled to open in 2027.

sources.news_title: Buc-ee’s CEO: ‘Conservative states’ get stores — here are the three key requirements
sources.text:
Buc-ee’s CEO says ‘conservative’ states will get stores — and there are three requirements any location must meet
Texas-based Buc-ee’s now operates in at least a dozen states, which are primarily Republican-leaning or conservative
The CEO of Buc-ee’s says the beloved convenience chain will focus expansion on conservative states as the beaver-themed brand faces scrutiny over its repeated trademark lawsuits.
Arch “Beaver” Aplin III, also the Texas chain’s co-founder, made the remarks last week during the grand opening of Buc-ee’s first Arkansas location in Benton.
"We have a lot of opportunities. We're growing. We're building in a lot of places, but when you find a conservative, business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference," Aplin said in a video shared by Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders on social media.
"And I'm starting to realize life's too short to try to build in places that people don't appreciate what you're bringing versus a place like this, where people do appreciate what you're building,” Aplin added.
He then explained that Buc-ee’s-worthy locations must meet three of the brand’s key values.
"So that leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept works so much better if it trickles down from the very leadership," Aplin said. "From the very top at the governor's office, at the congressman, at the senator, at the mayor (and) the representatives."
Sanders, who previously served as White House press secretary under President Donald Trump, said in her caption that Aplin “said it best” about taking the chain where it is appreciated.
“That’s why red states like Arkansas are surging and people and businesses are fleeing blue state,” Sanders said.
Buc-ee’s began as a small convenience store in Lake Jackson, Texas, before opening its first massive travel center in 2003 in Luling, south of Austin. The chain expanded throughout Texas before making its first move beyond the state in 2019, opening in Loxley, Alabama.
Since then, Buc-ee’s has rapidly spread across the country, drawing a cult following with its famously clean restrooms, massive stores and branded merchandise. The chain now operates in at least a dozen states, primarily Republican-leaning ones, including Georgia, Florida, Kentucky, South Carolina, Tennessee, Missouri and Ohio, with plans to expand further.
However, Buc-ee’s currently faces a growing PR headache over trademark lawsuits, including a fight with a small Ohio corner store that has sparked calls for boycotts, fundraising and beaver-themed logos in solidarity.
On July 28, Buc-ee’s sued Beaver’s Mini Mart in Beavercreek, Ohio, arguing customers could confuse its logo with Buc-ee’s. The neighborhood store has no gas pumps and sits miles from the nearest interstate, but its logo features a smiling beaver alongside its name in red lettering.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has called the lawsuit “ridiculous” and urged Buc-ee’s to drop it.
The controversy grew after comedian John Oliver took aim at Buc-ee’s on “Last Week Tonight” last month, detailing the chain’s history of suing small businesses over cartoon animal logos. The cases include a 2014 Texas fight over a beaver logo, a 2015 lawsuit over a cartoon alligator, a February 2026 suit against a northern Ohio gas station over its Mickey the Moose logo, and a May 2026 suit against Georgia’s Teddy’s Market over its hat-wearing mascot.
Oliver then challenged Buc-ee’s to sue him over his support for Beaver’s Mini Mart, launching satirical “Buc-Off” merchandise featuring a squirrel logo parodying Buc-ee’s branding, with proceeds going to charity.
Earlier this month, Beavercreek City Council officially recognized the beaver as a historic city symbol, allowing local businesses, schools and organizations to continue using beaver imagery amid the trademark fight with Buc-ee’s.
The Independent has contacted Buc-ee’s for comment.

sources.news_title: Buc-ee’s CEO Signals Shift Toward Business-Friendly ‘Red’ States
Buc-ee’s CEO Signals Shift Toward Business-Friendly 'Red' States
sources.text:
Buc-ee’s may be narrowing its expansion focus as the Texas-based travel center chain continues its rapid growth across the country.
Arch “Beaver” Aplin III, Buc-ee’s co-founder, president, and CEO, said during the August 17 grand opening of the company’s newest location in Benton, Arkansas, that right-leaning, business-friendly communities are increasingly attractive to the company.
“We have a lot of opportunities. We’re growing. We’re building in a lot of places, but when you find a conservative, business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference,” Aplin said.
He also suggested the company may be less interested in communities where local leaders do not appreciate the economic development Buc-ee’s brings.
“I’m starting to realize life’s too short to try to build in places that people don’t appreciate what you’re bringing versus a place like this, where people do appreciate what you’re building,” Aplin said.
Buc-ee’s Looks For Business-Friendly Communities
Aplin said the company’s experience in Benton demonstrated the value of having supportive local leadership.
He described the city as a “business-friendly town” and said the company’s preferred approach works best when support extends from state leadership to local officials.
Buc-ee’s is known for its large travel centers, extensive fueling operations, food offerings, and highly regarded restrooms. The company says its typical locations span about 74,000 square feet and include 120 fueling positions, with many locations creating more than 200 jobs.
The chain currently has 58 locations, including 37 in Texas, and has expanded into 13 other states.
Expansion Continues Across The Country
Despite Aplin’s comments about where the company prefers to build, Buc-ee’s expansion plans remain broad.
The company is scheduled to open a new location in Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on November 16.
Additional locations listed by Buc-ee’s include six planned openings in 2027:
- Ruston, Louisiana
- Kansas City, Kansas
- Gallaway, Tennessee
- St. Lucie, Florida
- Boerne, Texas
- Monroe County, Georgia
Two more locations are listed for 2028 in Mebane, North Carolina, and Lafayette, Louisiana.
Buc-ee’s also lists planned projects in Ocala, Florida; West Memphis, Arkansas; and Oak Grove, Kentucky, for 2029, along with a Hardeeville, South Carolina, location planned for 2031.
The company has recently expanded into new markets, opening its first locations in Ohio and Arizona in 2026 after entering Virginia in 2025 and Colorado in 2024.
Texas Roots Remain Central
Founded in 1982, Buc-ee’s has become one of Texas’ best-known retail and travel brands. Its continued expansion has taken the company well beyond the state, but most of its locations remain in Texas.
The chain’s growth has also brought it into communities with varying political landscapes. While many Buc-ee’s locations are in areas that generally lean Republican, some are located in communities with more politically mixed or Democratic-leaning local dynamics.
Aplin’s comments indicate that local and state leadership could play a larger role in where the company chooses to establish future locations as its national expansion continues.
For now, Buc-ee’s has a substantial pipeline of new stores extending through the next several years, with locations planned across the South and Midwest as the company continues expanding its Texas-born travel center model.

sources.news_title: 'Conservative, business-friendly states:' Buc-ee's CEO wants to avoid Blue states
sources.text:
If you’ve driven on the interstate throughout the southeastern portion of the United States, you’ve likely encountered a Buc-ee’s travel center. Buc-ee’s currently has locations in 13 different U.S. states, and while the chain is continually expanding, it doesn’t sound like they’ll be moving into Blue states anytime soon.
During a recent speech, Buc-ee’s founder and CEO Arch “Beaver” Aplin III made it pretty clear that as the massive travel center expands, it will prioritize “conservative, business-friendly” states.
What is Buc-ee’s?
Founded in Texas in 1982, Buc-ee’s is a massive, highly popular American chain of mega-travel centers and convenience stores found on the side of interstates. The massive travel centers have become known for having dozens of fueling positions, notoriously clean and large restrooms, and an enormous selection of food and beaver-themed merchandise.
The massive travel centers include over 100 fuel pumps and a massive market that rivals the size of some supermarkets. Unlike most other travel centers, Buc-ee’s also bans semi-trucks, prioritizing travelers in cars and smaller personal vehicles.
Currently, Buc-ee’s exists in 13 different U.S. states: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Mississippi, Missouri, Ohio, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Texas.
‘Conservative, business-friendly states’
With Buc-ee’s opening a new location in Benton, Arkansas, Alpin gave a speech where he opened up a little bit about why Buc-ee’s chooses to open its stores where they do.
While he acknowledged that Buc-ee’s is expanding to “a lot of places,” he also made it pretty clear that the company will prioritize red states over blue states.
“We’re growing. We’re building in a lot of places. But when you find a conservative, business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference. And I’m starting to realize life’s too short to try to build in places that people don’t appreciate what you’re bringing, versus a place like this where people do appreciate what you’re building,” Aplin said in a video shared by Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
Of the 13 states where Buc-ee’s currently has at least one location, only one of those states – Colorado – is a solidly blue state. Aplin made it pretty clear that this is no accident.
“That leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept, works so much better if it trickles down from the leadership, from the very top of the governor’s office, at the congressmen, at the senators, at the mayors, the representatives. And so, what we found when we got here in Benton (Arkansas) was a business-friendly town,” he added. “They said ‘Let’s roll up our sleeves and let’s go get a Buc-ee’s built.'”
Needless to say, if you live in a blue state and are waiting for a Buc-ee’s location near you, you might be waiting a long time.

About a year and change ago, we wrote a piece about the states that will probably never get a Buc-ee’s. Most of the states we mentioned had either low population, logistical or environmental concerns (or sometimes more than one of those) that would most likely prevent a Buc-ee’s from ever opening in each state.
However, although Buc-ee’s continues to expand (these are the places most recently announced to get a store in the not-too-distant future), it now appears that several other states may have just landed on the “probably never getting a Buc-ee’s” list.
And this time, it has nothing to do with population, logistics or the environment.
Just politics.
During a recent speech, Buc-ee’s founder and CEO Arch “Beaver” Aplin III made it pretty clear that as the massive travel center expands, it will prioritize “conservative, business-friendly” states.
A new Buc-ee’s was opening in Benton, Arkansas and Alpin gave a speech that included a part of the “secret sauce” of where they open new stores.
“We’re growing. We’re building in a lot of places. But when you find a conservative, business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference. And I’m starting to realize life’s too short to try to build in places that people don’t appreciate what you’re bringing, versus a place like this where people do appreciate what you’re building,” Aplin said in a video that was shared by Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
And if you research a little, you’ll see that of the 13 states where Buc-ee’s currently has at least one location, only one – Colorado – is a solidly blue state.
And Aplin certainly didn’t hide his preference for the alternative.
“That leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept, works so much better if it trickles down from the leadership, from the very top of the governor’s office, at the congressmen, at the senators, at the mayors, the representatives. And so, what we found when we got here in Benton (Arkansas) was a business-friendly town,” he added. “They said ‘Let’s roll up our sleeves and let’s go get a Buc-ee’s built.’”
Of course, since Buc-ee’s is a privately owned company, Aplin can do as he pleases with his company. But intentionally avoiding “blue” states would certainly seem shortsighted from a business perspective.
I mean, Democrats have just as much need for clean bathrooms and presumably would want to buy drinks, snacks, beaver merchandise and cheap gasoline after they pee, just as much as Republicans do.
But I wonder if some of what he’s saying is just sour grapes.
I mean, as we said in an earlier post, California has strict environmental standards and the rules Buc-ee’s would need to follow in the name of sustainability alone, might be more than they’d be willing to invest. Massachusetts has zoning laws the company would have to follow. In New Jersey, the law is that someone has to pump your gas for you.
So it’s possible that when Alpin says he wants to focus on “conservative, business-friendly” states, that’s his secret code for “liberal states have laws that won’t let me do things the way I want to do them.”
Aplin’s speech also doesn’t explain Colorado, where Buc-ee’s opened its first location in 2024 despite the state hardly fitting the political description he just praised.
So does Aplin really not want to open Buc-ee’s travel centers in liberal states?
Or is “conservative, business-friendly” actually shorthand for places where Buc-ee’s can build and operate the way Buc-ee’s wants to?
What this means for travelers
Whatever the answer, Aplin’s comments certainly make it sound as if Buc-ee’s expansion map isn’t based solely on population, highway traffic and finding a big enough piece of land anymore. Politics (or at least what Buc-ee’s considers a favorable political and business environment) is apparently part of the equation, too.
Which means that if you live in a solidly blue state (not including Colorado) and have been patiently waiting for Buc-ee’s to eventually make its way to you, well…you may be waiting a very, very long time.
And that’s a shame.
Not because of the brisket. Or the Beaver Nuggets. Or the jerky. Or even the ridiculously large selection of Buc-ee the Beaver merchandise.
It’s the bathrooms.
Because political affiliation aside, there are certain things Americans should be able to come together on. And surely a gigantic, ridiculously clean highway bathroom with enough stalls that you never have to wait in line can be one of them.
Republican, Democrat, independent…when you’ve been on the interstate for three hours and really have to pee, we are all the same.
And perhaps that should be Buc-ee’s real expansion policy. 😉
